title: HIV Nursing Care: Testing, ART, Opportunistic Infections & Exposure Management
html:
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) targets CD4 cells and can progressively weaken cell-mediated immunity when it is not effectively treated. Modern antiretroviral therapy (ART) can suppress viral replication, preserve immune function, prevent sexual transmission when suppression is sustained, and allow people with HIV to live long lives. The RN combines accurate testing, stigma-free communication, medication and interaction safety, opportunistic-infection surveillance, Standard Precautions, and rapid post-exposure response.

Learning goals

  • Explain the HIV testing algorithm and the limits of testing during the window period.
  • Differentiate HIV RNA viral load from CD4 count and use trends to evaluate treatment and immune risk.
  • Support prompt ART, adherence, interaction screening, and respectful shared decision-making.
  • Recognize urgent patterns of Pneumocystis pneumonia and neurologic opportunistic infection.
  • Apply Standard Precautions and initiate occupational post-exposure management without delay.
  • Use precise U=U counseling while protecting privacy and reducing stigma.

Testing follows an algorithm

Laboratory diagnosis generally begins with an HIV-1/2 antigen-antibody combination assay. A repeatedly reactive screen is followed by an HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation assay. When results are discordant or indeterminate, or when acute infection is suspected before antibodies have developed, an HIV nucleic acid test (NAT) helps identify acute infection and distinguish a false-positive screen. A reactive screening result alone is not the final diagnosis.

Ask when the possible exposure occurred, what test was used, whether symptoms compatible with acute retroviral illness are present, and whether antiretroviral medicines were used as PEP or PrEP. A negative result obtained too early may not exclude infection because every test has a window period. Follow the current testing algorithm and arrange repeat or NAT testing when indicated rather than offering false reassurance. Explain each step, obtain consent as required, preserve confidentiality, and never test or disclose casually.

ART is recommended for all people with HIV

Current federal guidance recommends ART for everyone with HIV and starting as soon as possible after diagnosis. Rapid initiation improves health and reduces onward transmission, but the exact regimen requires review of resistance results, kidney and liver function, hepatitis B status, pregnancy considerations, comorbidities, medicines and supplements, and access. Do not delay linkage to care while assuming the patient must first become perfectly adherent.

Reconcile the exact drug names, doses, timing, food instructions, antacids or mineral supplements, and other interactions. Ask about missed doses without blame: cost, transportation, housing, privacy, depression, substance use, nausea, pill burden, and schedule complexity may all be solvable barriers. Do not advise abruptly stopping or intermittently taking the whole regimen. Some ART components also suppress hepatitis B, so unplanned discontinuation can cause hepatitis flare. Use the regimen-specific plan or pharmacist for missed doses and interactions.

Viral load and CD4 answer different questions

HIV RNA viral load measures circulating virus and is the primary marker of ART response. Effective therapy should produce and maintain viral suppression. CD4 count estimates immune function and helps assess susceptibility to opportunistic infections, determine selected prophylaxis needs, and follow immune recovery. A patient can have an undetectable viral load while the CD4 count recovers gradually; the two tests are not interchangeable.

At entry to care, anticipate ordered viral load, CD4 count, resistance testing, blood count, kidney and liver tests, hepatitis screening, tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infection evaluation, pregnancy testing when relevant, immunization review, and other individualized studies. If viral load remains detectable or rebounds, verify the result and assess adherence, access, intolerance, interactions, absorption, and resistance with the team. A detectable value is clinical information—not evidence of a character flaw.

U=U is prevention science, not a cure

Undetectable equals untransmittable (U=U) means that a person who takes ART as prescribed and maintains an undetectable viral load has zero risk of sexually transmitting HIV. Use the word sexual precisely. Viral suppression does not eradicate HIV, replace continued ART and monitoring, prevent other sexually transmitted infections, or prevent pregnancy. When suppression has not yet been confirmed or maintained, discuss condoms, partner testing, PrEP, and other prevention options according to the patient's goals.

Opportunistic infections require pattern recognition

Risk depends on immune status, exposure, geography, prior infection, prophylaxis, and ART response. Prophylaxis is selected from CD4 count, viral load, serology, history, and the current guideline; it is not one blanket medicine for every person with HIV. Verify the indication, allergies, kidney and liver function, interactions, adherence, and the criteria for starting or stopping prophylaxis.

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) often develops subacutely with progressive dyspnea, fever, nonproductive cough, chest discomfort, tachypnea, or exertional desaturation, especially with advanced immunosuppression. Resting lung findings may be modest despite important hypoxemia. Escalate increasing work of breathing or falling oxygen saturation, provide authorized oxygen, obtain ordered imaging and blood-gas or microbiologic studies, and prepare prompt treatment. Do not wait for dramatic crackles.

New severe or persistent headache, fever, confusion, behavior change, seizure, focal deficit, or reduced consciousness requires urgent CNS evaluation. Cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, tuberculosis, bacterial infection, stroke, malignancy, and medication or metabolic causes may overlap. Protect the airway and seizure safety, assess intracranial-pressure risk, obtain urgent specialist evaluation, and do not delay stabilization for a complete diagnostic label. Pulmonary tuberculosis suspicion requires airborne precautions because of TB—not because HIV itself requires isolation.

IRIS can look like treatment failure

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is inflammatory worsening of a known infection or the new presentation of a previously unrecognized infection after immune recovery begins on ART. Timing, symptoms, CD4 and viral-load trends, infection testing, and medication history help the team distinguish IRIS from a new or uncontrolled infection, treatment failure, drug toxicity, or another disease. Report deterioration urgently and continue supportive assessment; do not independently stop ART or antimicrobial therapy.

HIV alone does not require special isolation

Use Standard Precautions for every patient: hand hygiene; gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection according to the anticipated exposure; injection and sharps safety; respiratory hygiene; and appropriate cleaning and handling of equipment and linen. Routine touching, sharing a room, delivering food, or using the same toilet does not transmit HIV. Add Contact, Droplet, or Airborne Precautions only when another suspected or confirmed condition requires them.

Keep HIV status out of public boards and casual conversation. Share information only with people authorized to participate in care and according to law and policy. Use person-first language such as “person with HIV,” ask preferred terms, explore goals and barriers, and correct myths without shaming. Stigma can drive avoidance of testing and treatment and is itself a safety risk.

PEP is time-critical

After an occupational needlestick, cut, splash to mucous membrane, or significant exposure to nonintact skin, wash skin with soap and water and flush mucous membranes with water. Do not squeeze the wound, use bleach or caustic chemicals, or delay reporting. Notify the designated occupational-health or exposure service immediately, document the route and material, assess the source under law and policy, and obtain baseline testing.

When PEP is indicated, begin it as soon as possible—ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours. Do not delay the first dose while waiting for every laboratory result or source result. The usual course is 28 days, with regimen review for kidney function, pregnancy, interactions, and tolerability. Arrange follow-up HIV testing, adverse-effect support, and counseling. If exposure risk is ongoing, plan a clinician-guided transition from PEP to PrEP rather than extending PEP informally.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify exposure timing, test type, viral-load and CD4 trends, ART and prophylaxis, respiratory or neurologic symptoms, adherence barriers, and possible medication interactions.
  2. Analyze cues: Connect subacute dyspnea and hypoxemia with possible PCP; compare CNS infection, stroke, toxicity, and metabolic disease; and distinguish a screening result from a completed diagnostic algorithm.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Respiratory failure, sepsis, altered consciousness, seizure, focal neurologic change, severe medication reaction, and a time-sensitive blood exposure outrank routine teaching.
  4. Generate solutions: Stabilize airway and oxygenation, obtain ordered diagnostic studies, initiate the exposure pathway, reconcile ART and interactions, and involve HIV, infectious-disease, pharmacy, respiratory, and social-support resources.
  5. Take action: Use appropriate precautions, administer authorized ART, antimicrobial therapy, prophylaxis or PEP on time, protect confidentiality, and address barriers without blame.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm viral suppression, immune recovery, improving oxygenation and neurologic status, completed PEP follow-up, safe medication use, and the patient's ability to explain warning signs and the care plan.

Clinical example

A patient with HIV who has been off ART presents with one week of worsening dyspnea, dry cough, fever, and oxygen saturation of 86% on room air. The RN recognizes possible PCP but does not stop at one hypothesis. The RN supports oxygenation, assesses work of breathing and hemodynamics, applies additional precautions only if another transmissible condition such as pulmonary TB is suspected, obtains ordered imaging and diagnostic specimens, and promptly communicates the ART history, CD4 and viral-load data, prophylaxis history, and clinical trend. Stabilization and evidence-based treatment proceed while the team evaluates PCP, bacterial or viral pneumonia, TB, pulmonary embolism, and other causes.

HIV testing, ART, prophylaxis, opportunistic-infection treatment, isolation for concurrent infection, PEP, PrEP, pregnancy care, and disclosure obligations require current patient data, authorized orders, jurisdictional law, local protocols, and specialist or occupational-health guidance.
